This report summarizes and reflects on the laboratory assignments and lectures completed in the Large Language Models and Generative AI for NLP course. 
Through a series of hands-on labs, theoretical concepts introduced in the lectures were applied to practical tasks involving for example prompt design, evaluation and fine-tuning.

The purpose of the report is to describe what was done in each lab, explain the motivation behind the chosen solutions, and highlight key aspects learned during the course.
The report also reflects on challenges encountered when working with LLMs, such as technical difficulties during different tasks.

All code implementations used for the weekly work and experiments are available in the GitHub repository Noraelisa/LLM-course-2025 (<https://github.com/Noraelisa/LLM-course-2025>), 
organized in folders according to the weekly lab structure.

The report is organized by weeks, followed by a concluding section that summarizes overall insights gained from the weekly lectures and work done on the lab assignments.

# Week 1 - Introduction to language models

Week 1 we had an introduction to Large Language Models and Generative AI. 
I do have general knowledge in language models, but not a deep understanding of
Large Language Models or Generative LLMs. What I learned from the first lecture:

The term language model refers to a task of estimating the probability distribution of sequences of
tokens (words) in a given language. The model learns which word combinations are more likely
than others, in other words it tries to figure out what words are most likely to come after next.

The model assigns a probability to the entire sequence, formally conditional probability of the
next word $w_1w_1...w_n$ given the previous words:

$P(w_n \mid w_1 w_2 \dots w_{n-1})$

Language modelling aims to capture patterns and structure of a language, so it is able to 
predict which words are likely to come next or generate new sentences that sounds natural language.

Popular language models are for example, **N-gram models**, **Hidden Markov Models (HHM)**, **Word Embeddings (Word2vec)**
and **transformer models**. **N-gram models** predicts next word based on the last n words. **HMMs** treat language
as sequences of hidden states that produces words, each state depends on the one before (Markov property).
**Word Embeddings** turns words into numerical vectors so the model can understand relationships between
words, words that are similar in meaning are closer in the vector space. **Transformer models** uses attention
mechanisms to look at all words in sentence at once, which helps it the models to understand context
and meaning better.

**Transformer models** are a type of neural network architecture designed for natural language processing (NLP).
They use self-attention to see how each word relates to all the others in a sentence. Self-attention helps
the model understand context and long-range connections. Since self-attention alone does not hold knowledge 
to the word order, a positional encodings are added to input embeddings (numerical vectors) which tells 
the model the word order. Transformers are built from encoder and decoder layers, each layer containing
self-attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections and layer normalization, enabling efficient parallel 
processing and stable training. **Feed-forward network** transforms each word's representation to capture complex
patterns. **Residual connections** are a shortcut paths that helps to train deep networks without loosing information.
**Layer normalization** keeps numbers stable for faster ans more reliable training. Together these components
in every layer makes transformers efficient ans stable.

There are three main variants of transformers:

- Encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) focus on understanding text for tasks like classification or named entity recognition.

- Decoder-only models (e.g., GPT, LLaMA) specialize in generating text, predicting words one at a time for tasks like text generation and summarization.

- Encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5, BART) combine understanding and generation, making them suitable for machine translation, summarization, and dialogue systems.

## Lab Assignment 1 - Tokenizers

**Description of the lab**:

Research on Tokenizers and write a section to your final report reflecting on the following questions:

- What are tokenizers?
- Why are they important for language modeling and LLMs?
- What different tokenization algorithms are there and which ones are the most popular ones and why?

**Answer**:

Tokenizers take text as an input and breaks it down into smaller units, called tokens. The tokens
are words, parts of words or individual characters. Tokenizers convert the tokens into numerical 
values which the language model can process.

"This is a sample text" -> Tokenizer -> ["This", "is", "a", "sample", "text"]

As mentioned before, tokenizers are important for language models and Large Language Models by the
ability to make the text understandable to the models. Since models work with numerical values, not 
raw text. Due to tokenizers, different languages and symbols can be handled by the models, for example
non-Latin scripts (Arabic, Chinese) or emojis. The models quality or performance is influenced by 
how the text is tokenized, since it can change how the model sees contextual boundaries and relationships
between words. The better the tokenizers (fewer tokens) faster the models processing.

Different tokenization algorithms are Word-based Tokenizers, Character-based Tokenizers, Subword-based
Tokenizers and Byte-level Tokenizer.

> **Word-based Tokenizers** - Splits text by spaces and punctuation. It is very simple and easy to implements, although
> it can lead to problems while processing large text corpora or rare words, contractions and languages without spaces.

> **Character-based Tokenizers** - Splits text into individual characters. It is very simple and efficient, but
> it makes it harder for the model to understand meaning, since token carries very little information.

> **Subword-based Tokenizers** - Splits text into smaller, frequent parts, meaning that frequently used words
> should not be split into smaller subwords, but more rare words should. It balances vocabulary size while being able
> to learn the meaning of word parts.

Most popular tokenization algorithms today are probably Byte-Level BPE, WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece. They all
provids a good balance between efficiency, flexibility and language coverage.
  
> **Byte-Level BPE** splits text into subwords based on how often pairs of letters or symbols appear together.
> It works on byte level, allowing the model to handled any language, symbol or emoji (all unicode characters).
> It is used in GPT-2 and later models, since its flexile and efficient.
> 
> **WordPiece** is similar to BPE, but it 
> chooses the best subwords using probabilities instead of just frequency. It helps the model to understand parts 
> of words and handle rare or new words, it is used in BERT, since it helps to capture meanigful word patterns.
> 
> **Unigram** in contrast starts with large set of symbols and gradually remoces the least important ones to create
> smaller ans efficient vocabulary. It doesn't merge any letter or subwords, allowing it to split words in different
> valid ways using the subwords. It tracks how likely each subword is based on the training data. Unigram is not used
> directry for any models, but is is used together with **SentencePiece**, which is a framework that can use either
> BPE or unigram algortihm to construct appropriate vocabulary.


# Week 2 - Prompting

Week 2 we digged into the topic of prompt engineering. Prompting is a action of providing an instructions, also known
as inputs, to a pre-trained large language model to guide the models response or outputs. It is a way to 
"communicate" with the model, the prompt tells the model what you want it to do, how to do it and possibly in which
style or format. Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining inputs given to the model in order to
guide its behavior and produce the most accurate, relevant or creative outputs.

>> Instructions/Promt: "Write a short story about two dogs playing with a sock."
>> Response: The model generates a story about the topic.

Prompting guides the model towards the output what you desire. To leverage the emergent capabilities of LLMs, tailored
promts to a specific tasks ables the model to write poems or geretate code. By prompting we are able to control the expected
output, for example length, style or format of the output. Prompting improves efficiency and creativity, so that the model 
is able to adapt to new tasks quickly and lead to suprising and insightful outputs.

To make prompts more effective, different prompting techniques are used. In the lecture we went through for example; Zero-Shot prompting,
Few-Shot prompting and Chain-of-Thought (CoT).

> **Zero-Shot Prompting**: The model is not given any prior examples, just clear instructions or question, by leveraging the skills learned
> during pre-training.
> 
>> **Prompt**: Translate this English sentence into Finnish: Three little piggies went to the market.
>> **Output**: Kolme pientä porsasta meni torille.
>
> **Few-Shot Prompting**: The model is given few examples of how you want it to behave before asking for the result.
>
>> **Prompt**: Do a sentiment analysis on the given sentence. I hate bananas: negative;I love dogs: positive;Today I 
> like apples: positive; I love doing LLM courses exercises:
>>  **Answer**: positive
>
> **Chain-Of-Thought (CoT) Prompting**: CoT enables the model to do complex resoning through intemediate reasoning steps.
>
>> **Prompt**: If a train travels 60 km in 1 hour, how long will it take to travel 150 km? Let’s solve this step by step
>> **Answer**: Speed is 60km/h and distance 150km. Time=Distance/Soeed=150/60=2.5hours. Final answer: 2.5 hours.
>
> **Prompt Chaining**: The larger or more complex tasks are splitted into smaller steps, where each step's output becomes
> the next step's input.
>
>> **Prompt 1**: List 3 startup ideas related to renewable energy.
>>> **Answer 1**: Solar-powered drones, smart wind turbines, AI for energy grids.
>> **Prompt 2**: Pick the most promising idea and create a business plan.
>>> **Answer 2**: Business plan for “AI for energy grids".

# Week 3 - Evaluation

In week 3 the topic of the lecture and lab assignment was about evaluation in LLMs. This week we learned about evaluation of Large Language Models,
focusing on how to determine whether an LLM is performing well and what “good performance” actually means. I had a general idea that models are
tested using benchmarks, but I did not fully understand the different evaluation types or the many dimensions involved in assessing LLM quality.
What I learned from this lecture:

Evaluation refers to assessing how well a model performs a specific task. There are different forms of
evaluation:

> **Intrinsic**: Testing the model on isolated tasks such as language quality, reasoning, or coherence.
>
> **Extrinsic**: Testing how the model performs as part of a real-world application.
> 
> **Monitoring vs. quality assurance**: Ongoing tracking versus pre-deployment validation.

A key idea is that every evaluation depends on the use case. An LLM might perform well in writing tasks,
but poorly in legal reasoning or safety-critical decision-making. Therefore, performance must always be
interpreted relative to the model’s intended function. LLMs are often assessed using benchmarks,
which provide standardized tasks and allow comparison across models. Classical evaluation metrics such as **precision**,
**recall**, **accuracy**, and **true/false positive rates** come from classification tasks, but many evaluation ideas for LLMs still draw on these concepts.

In the lecture several top-level quality criteria were introduced that go beyond accuracy.
These include:

> **Effectiveness**: Speed, computational efficiency
>
> **Compliance**: Following safety rules, regulations
>
> **Linguistic quality**: Grammar and fluency
>
> **Consistency**: Stable responses across variations of input
>
> **Topical competence**: Domain knowledge
>
> **Veracity**: Truthfulness
>
> **Discourse coherence** across multiple turns
>
> **Creativity and ability** to generate interesting output
> 
> **Social awareness and politeness**
>
> **Common sense reasoning**

In the lecture variety of modern evaluation benchmarks were introduced,
each of which probes different abilities:

> **Hyperbaton**: Adjective ordering
> 
> **Disambiguation QA**: Pronoun resolution
>
> **HellaSwag**: Narrative plausibility
>
> **BBQ**: Bias and social reasoning
> 
> **ARC**: Scientific reasoning
> 
> **MT Bench** Complex instruction following

These evaluation methods shows that evaluating LLMs covers linguistic structure, reasoning, world knowledge, bias, and more.

One important insight from the lecture is that linguistic ability and world knowledge can't easily be separated.
When a model fails a test, it is hard to know whether the cause is linguistic limitation or missing factual knowledge.
Cultural assumptions within benchmarks also influence outcomes, meaning that tests often need adaptation for different languages and societies.

LLMs are trained to produce plausible text, not necessarily truthful text. This can lead to issues such as:

> **Sycophancy**, agreeing with the user even when wrong
>
> **Confident misinformation**
> 
> **Over-aligning** with user expectations instead of factual accuracy

Because of this, evaluation must take into account not just how fluent the model is,
but how grounded, consistent, and socially appropriate its output is.

**Conclusion**:

**Is there a difference between responses in two languages? In how many questions?**

Looking at the table, Finnish vs. English answers are essentially translations of the same idea (same advice/content) for each matching variant pair, so there are 0 questions with a meaningful language-driven difference.

**Is there less difference if the questions are localised? In how many questions?**

Same result: within each locale pair (Finland: C vs F, US: D vs G, Saudi: E vs H), the answers are also content-equivalent translations, so 0 questions show less/more difference due to localization in the language pair (because there wasn’t language-driven divergence to begin with).

**Entertaining responses or differences worth noting**

The interesting differences are by locale (culture), not by language. A few notable ones to mention:

- Dinner time (Q10): Finland earlier (18–19), US (18–20), Saudi later (20–22).

- Easter food (Q8): Finland/US have typical Easter foods, but Saudi: “not traditionally celebrated.”

- Dating (Q3): Finland/US emphasize apps/social events; Saudi emphasizes family/social networks.

- Tipping (Q11): Finland optional, US 10–15%, Saudi optional but appreciated.

- LGBTQ question (Q6): Finland/US suggest seeking support; Saudi versions add extra caution about who to tell (more safety-focused).

- Breakfast (Q1): Finland (porridge/rye bread), US (cereal/toast), Saudi (bread/eggs/yogurt/fruit).

Overall, the dataset suggests that language (Finnish vs. English) did not materially change the guidance, since the answers
were mostly direct translations. The largest differences came from localization, where the same question was framed through local habits, norms, and expectations.
A few localized outputs were especially notable because they reflected cultural context and
practical safety considerations, which is exactly what the locale variants were designed to capture.

# Week 4 - Fine-tuning

In week 4 the topic of the lecture and lab assignment was about Fine-tuning. In the lecture difference between prompting and fine-tuning was discussed.
Prompting and fine-tuning are two different ways of adapting a language model.
- **Prompting** does not change the model itself; instead, we guide the model by giving well-designed instructions that influence how it responds.
- **Fine-tuning** updates the model’s internal parameters using task-specific data, allowing it to learn a task more accurately and consistently than prompting alone.
  fine-tuning os used when we need stronger task performance, better reliability, or when prompting is not enough. It works by taking a pre-trained model,
  training it further on a targeted dataset, and adjusting the weights slightly with a small learning rate across a few training epochs.

The lecture introduced several fine-tuning methods.
- **Supervised fine-tuning** uses labeled input–output pairs to teach the model a direct task.
- **Instruction tuning** trains the model on various instructions and desired outputs so it can follow natural-language prompts more effectively.
- **RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)** improves the model using human judgments about which outputs are better.
- **DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)** simplifies this by directly learning from pairs of preferred and rejected responses.

In the lecture PEFT and quantization was discussed, where both aim to make working with large language models more efficient;
- **Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** makes the process cheaper and lighter by updating only a small set of added parameters—such as LoRA layers, prefix tokens, or adapter layers—rather than retraining the whole model.
- **Quantization** reduces the precision of model weights (for example, from 32-bit to 8-bit), which shrinks the model size and speeds up inference with only a small performance loss.

**Description of the lab**:

Run the supervised_finetuning.ipynb in Google Colab (convert to python script)

**Answer**:

The model was fine-tuned on a subset of **10,000 training examples** (intentionally limited to reduce compute time). Training was performed for **1 epoch**, resulting in a final training loss of **1.29** and a mean token accuracy of **0.65** (65%).
These results indicate that the model has begun to learn meaningful patterns from the data, although performance remains preliminary due to limited training time, small dataset size, and only **4 gradient update steps** (the moment when the model changes internal weights to learn from data).

Overall, the observed metrics are consistent with an early fine-tuning stage and are **not yet sufficient** to evaluate final model quality. More epochs, a larger dataset, and repeated evaluation will be required to determine true downstream performance.

The GPT-4 version provides higher-quality responses but may introduce stylistic bias from GPT-4, whereas the cleaned Alpaca dataset offers more consistent formatting and fewer errors.

I will fine-tune the smaller **SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct** model to evaluate whether a lightweight (<7B) architecture can achieve usable performance with faster training and lower resource requirements compared to the previous model.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 is a larger and more capable 7B parameter model that delivers stronger performance and reasoning, but requires more compute and memory to fine-tune.
In contrast, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct is a much smaller 1.7B parameter model that is faster to train and easier to run on limited hardware like Google Colab,
but produces simpler outputs.

During fine-tuning, the model initially ran into CUDA out-of-memory issues on the Colab T4 GPU. By reducing the batch size to 7, the memory usage dropped enough for training to run successfully.

**Conclusion**:

Mistral-7B with the alpaca-gpt4 dataset achieved a lower training loss (1.29 vs. 1.55) and higher token accuracy (0.65 vs. 0.61),
indicating better learning and model capacity. However, the smaller SmolLM2-1.7B model trained much faster (22s vs. 69s) and
was significantly easier to run without memory issues. Overall, Mistral offers better performance, while SmolLM2 is the more
practical choice for low-resource environments like Google Colab.

There were a few practical challenges during the fine-tuning process. The first issue was logging into Hugging Face in Google Colab,
as token authentication repeatedly failed and produced permission errors. To resolve this, I manually passed the token as an environment variable.

Another major challenge was GPU memory limitations, even when using the smaller model. This required several adjustments, including reducing the batch size to 7.
These changes slowed training but ultimately made it possible to complete an epoch within the available memory.

# Week 5 - Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)

Week 5 focused on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a practical solution to some of the core limitations of Large Language Models, particularly hallucinations,
lack of up-to-date knowledge, and missing citations. The lecture explained how RAG combines information retrieval with text generation,
allowing an LLM to ground its answers in external documents retrieved via embeddings and vector search.

A key insight from the lecture was that RAG is often a simpler and more interpretable alternative to fine-tuning, especially when dealing with frequently
changing or domain-specific data. The lecture covered different RAG architectures (naive, advanced, and modular), the role of embeddings and approximate nearest
neighbor (ANN) search, and practical techniques such as chunking, reranking, metadata filtering, and evaluation metrics for RAG systems.

Another important takeaway was the introduction of agentic RAG, where autonomous agents can plan, retrieve, evaluate, and refine answers iteratively,
making RAG systems more adaptive and suitable for complex, real-world tasks. Overall, the lecture emphasized that effective use of LLMs is not just model-driven but
requires substantial engineering, system design, and evaluation, reinforcing the idea that reliable LLM applications depend on well-designed pipelines rather than raw generation alone.

- Would the same embedding and LLM work for Finnish?

The original embedding model (all-mpnet-base-v2) is not multilingual, it is designed and trained for

two different embedding models paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2 and distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v2.

  - Based on MPNet
  - Better semantic accuracy
  - Better meaning preservation in long sentences
  - More robust to domain-specific language (like Finnish scientific terminology)

  - Slightly weaker for highly technical or long sentences
  - Sometimes merges similar concepts too aggressively

Wall time: 38.4 s*

Eventhough the distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v2 is faster, paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2 has better
accuracy. Therefore, I decided to use the paraphrase embedded model on this task.

ost modern LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, LLaMA 3.x, Mixtral) handle Finnish well. Therefore,
the LLM part does not need to change.
  
- What about extracting sentences and chunking: is there any change in terms of token length / chunk size?

The PDF shows a normal token density (~600 tokens per page), which is well suited for creating 400–600 token chunks with small overlap.
The page-level statistics confirm that most pages fall between 500–700 tokens, but the sentence counts are extremely inconsistent—ranging
from only a few sentences to more than 600 on OCR-damaged pages. This happens because OCR splits text at line breaks, Finnish hyphenation,
and recognition errors, making sentence-based chunking unreliable.

For this reason, chunking by token count is safer. The chunk-level statistics support this: although the chunking target was 400–600 tokens,
the actual chunks vary more widely due to noisy input, with a mean chunk size of about 155 tokens, some very small chunks (from OCR fragments),
and some large chunks. Even so, the majority of chunks fall into a usable range, and token-based chunking still produces far more stable and meaningful
segments than sentence-based chunking would in this document.

In total, the document produced 273 chunks. This is completely acceptable for a RAG system. Modern vector search can easily handle this scale,
and the LLM only uses a few top-k chunks per query. Since the chunk sizes are reasonably consistent on average—despite some noisy outliers, the
number of chunks does not harm retrieval or answer quality.

# Week 6 - Use cases and applications of LLMs

Week 6 explored how Large Language Models are used in real-world applications, focusing on moving from standalone models to complete systems.
The lecture covered practical use cases such as chat assistants, customer support automation, document search with RAG, natural language queries over
structured data, and synthetic data generation.

A key topic was multimodal LLMs, which combine text with images, audio, or video using specialized encoders and cross-modal attention, enabling richer
interaction beyond text alone. The lecture also highlighted the importance of vector databases and semantic search as core infrastructure for scalable
LLM applications.

Overall, the main insight was that effective LLM applications depend heavily on system design, combining models with retrieval, data, and tooling, rather
than relying solely on raw text generation.

Tasks 2. a-c are in the synthetic_data.py file.

2. d) Make misspellings capture a variety of error types (phonetic, omission, transposition, repetition)?
   
By defining all four errors as functions (omission, transpose, phonetic, repetition) and putting them into a list TYPO_FUNCS and
everytime a misspelling is created, one error is picked randomly. This means that over multiple generated misspellings,
each type is used at different times. By using randomness, it uses all error types over time, but might still get the 
same type several times in a row.

2. e) Test the resulting query variants with your favourite web search engine. Are results equal for the same for all variants of a given query? If not, why do you think this is happening?

| Original Query                                      | Misspelling                                               | Error Type        | Search Engine                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------------| 
| shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport     | shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airporrt          | Repetition        | Rome2erio, JFK airport, Blacklane   | 
| shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport     | shortest route to Times Square phrom JFK Airport          | Phonetic          | Rome2erio, JFK airport, Blacklane   |
| shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport     | shortest route to Times Squaer from JFK Airport           | Transposition     | Rome2erio, JFK airport, Blacklane   |
| shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport     | shortest route to Timez Square from JFK Airport           | Phonetic          | Rome2erio, JFK airport, Blacklane   |
| shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport     | shortest rooute to Times Square from JFK Airport          | Repetition        | Rome2erio, JFK airport, Blacklane   |

I tested each generated misspelling in Google. The results were always the same. But it always gave the right
correction of the sentence as "Näytetään tulokset haulle: shortest route to Times Square from JFK Airport".
This suggest that the search engine is able to correctly interpret the intended sentence even with typos in the query.
I was also thinking that, is it possible that the "JFK" makes the query easier for the search engine to interpret.
"JFK" is really well-known location entity, so even if the other words contain errors, the search engine can still understand the overall intent of the query. As a result,
the misspellings do not significantly change the search results.

# Final conclusion on the course

This course gave me a good first “touch point” to Large Language Models and how they function in practice.
Before, I had some general idea how they function, but now I understand much better how tokenization, transformers, prompting, evaluation, fine-tuning, and RAG all fit together.

I especially enjoyed trying different methods in the labs, and the evaluation assignment was surprisingly fun to work on. Comparing answers across languages and locales made the behaviour of LLMs feel much more concrete.

At the same time, I faced quite a lot of technical issues: Hugging Face token problems in Colab, the limitations of the free GPU, and the difficulty of doing anything heavy locally on my old MacBook Pro. Even though this was sometimes frustrating, it also forced me to learn more about practical tooling and workarounds.
It was rewarding to experiment with new environments, and getting the VSC extension for Colab to work felt like a small personal victory.

I also struggled at times with the lab instructions and course material. Some tasks felt unclear or open to interpretation, and in a few labs I did not fully understand what the expected outcome was or how exactly the LLM was supposed to be integrated.
More thorough or step-by-step guidance in certain parts would have helped, especielly when working with new tools.

Overall, the course was a useful and motivating introduction to working with LLMs in a more systematic way, and it gave me a good foundation to build on in future projects.
Despite the challenges, I had fun exploring the methods, and I now feel more confident experimenting with LLMs and related tools on my own.
